# All four assessments

```{r}
#| include: false
source(here::here("chapters", "_setup.R"))
# Fitted once by scripts/03_fit_models.R (R/results.R). Claims in the prose,
# like whether the effect lasts, are computed there too.
or_marginal <- results$or_marginal
or_conditional <- results$or_conditional
by_time <- results$by_time
lasts <- results$lasts
sd_patient <- results$sd_patient
```

## Proportion with sore throat over time

```{r}
#| label: fig-over-time
#| fig-cap: "Proportion of patients with any sore throat at rest, by arm and assessment."
props <- aggregate(any_pain ~ treatment + time, data = long, FUN = mean)
ggplot2::ggplot(props, ggplot2::aes(time, any_pain, colour = treatment, group = treatment)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) fmt_pct(x), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Any sore throat", colour = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

## Does the effect last?

The odds ratio at each assessment, from a GEE with a treatment-by-time
interaction. This analysis was added after the results were seen, when an
independent review found the client's question unanswered (D-009), so it is
post hoc and descriptive:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-by-time
#| tbl-cap: "Population-averaged odds ratio, licorice vs sugar, at each assessment (robust 95% CI)."
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Assessment = by_time$time,
    `Odds ratio (95% CI)` = fmt_or_cell(by_time$or, by_time$lower, by_time$upper),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
)
```

`r if (lasts) "The benefit persists to the first post-operative morning:" else "The benefit is not clear at every assessment:"`
odds ratios range from `r fmt_num(min(by_time$or), 2)` to
`r fmt_num(max(by_time$or), 2)`, and
`r if (lasts) "every" else "not every"` confidence interval excludes one
(largest upper limit `r fmt_num(max(by_time$upper), 2)`).

## One summary across assessments

Assuming a common odds ratio across the four assessments, licorice lowered
the odds of sore throat in the trial population (`r fmt_or(or_marginal)`;
`r fmt_p(or_marginal$p_value)`; GEE, D-003). The table above is the check on
that assumption.

## Why the mixed model gives a different number

The random-intercept model estimates `r fmt_or(or_conditional)`, much further
from one. This is not a contradiction. The estimated between-patient standard
deviation on the log-odds scale is `r fmt_num(sd_patient, 2)`, so some
patients are far more prone to sore throat than others. (Fitted by
adaptive quadrature, a change made after review because the Laplace
default is biased in this setting; D-008.) The mixed model's odds ratio
compares the same patient under each gargle; the GEE's compares the two
populations. The client's question is about populations, so the GEE
is the reported estimand (D-003, D-004).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
fit_warnings_note(
  results,
  c("GEE, common OR", "GEE, OR at each assessment", "Mixed model")
)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Where an AI assistant can go wrong here
Asked to "fit a mixed model and report the effect", an assistant will
happily report the conditional odds ratio as if it were the population
effect. The estimand is a statistical decision, which is why it is written
down in the plan and the decision record before the results.
:::
